Toward a Multidimensional CDI-CAT: Noun/Predicate Bias in American English

George Kachergis

2026-09-17

Motivation

A third replication of the noun/predicate bifactor CAT pipeline (Japanese: multidim/; Cantonese: multidim_cantonese/), this time on American English – both as a further cross-linguistic check and because English is the source CDI the Japanese form was translated from, making it a useful reference point. This is also the first language where the pipeline logic itself was factored out into multidim_pipeline/lib.R rather than copy-pasted, since a third from-scratch implementation was no longer justified.

items <- read_csv(here("multidim_english/item_lexical_categories.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
efa_loadings <- read_csv(here("multidim_english/efa2_loadings.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
bifactor_items <- read_csv(here("multidim_english/bifactor_item_params.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
bifactor_scores <- read_csv(here("multidim_english/bifactor_scores.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
  mutate(noun_predicate_bias = S1_noun - S2_predicate)
cat_summary <- read_csv(here("multidim_english/cat_simulation_summary.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
resp_data <- readRDS(here("multidim_english/noun_predicate_response_data.Rds"))
d_sub <- readRDS(here("multidim_english/modeling_subsample.Rds"))

jp_bifactor_scores <- read_csv(here("multidim/bifactor_scores.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
jp_items <- read_csv(here("multidim/item_lexical_categories.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
can_bifactor_scores <- read_csv(here("multidim_cantonese/bifactor_scores.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
  mutate(noun_predicate_bias = S1_noun - S2_predicate)
can_items <- read_csv(here("multidim_cantonese/item_lexical_categories.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)

1. Data, item classification, and a scale decision

English (American) WS has 8998 administrations on Wordbank after excluding non-producers and children at ceiling – 7-9x more than Japanese (939) or Cantonese (1205). Item classification uses the same category → class mapping (cross-validated against Wordbank’s own lexical_category, which again collapses verbs+adjectives into “predicates”), yielding 478 content items (312 noun, 166 predicate) – numerically identical to Japanese, unsurprising since the Japanese CDI:WS was translated from this instrument.

items %>%
  count(lexical_class, pos2) %>%
  arrange(pos2) %>%
  kable(col.names = c("Lexical class", "CAT dimension (pos2)", "N items"),
        caption = "English item counts by lexical class and CAT grouping.") %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
English item counts by lexical class and CAT grouping.
Lexical class CAT dimension (pos2) N items
noun noun 312
function_word other 102
other other 100
adjective predicate 63
verb predicate 103

Scale decision: fitting the EFA/bifactor models on the full ~9000-person sample would plausibly take hours (Cantonese, at 572 items x 1205 people, already took 30/12.6 min for EFA/bifactor; English at 478 items x 8998 people is ~7.5x more people). Rather than let that run unattended for an uncertain number of hours, a fixed random subsample of n = 1500 administrations (seed = 1234) was drawn and used consistently for the EFA, the confirmatory bifactor fit, and the CAT simulation’s full-item-bank comparison (all three must use the same people). This is a documented tractability decision – refitting on the full sample is a natural follow-up once the subsampled results are judged worth the extra compute, and it would only improve precision, not change the qualitative picture below.

2. Exploratory factor check

ggplot(efa_loadings, aes(x = F1, y = F2, color = pos2)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "F1 (general)", y = "F2 (noun vs. predicate)", color = "Item type",
       title = "English: exploratory 2-factor loadings") +
  theme_bw()

Third replication of the same signature: dominant general factor (mean F1 = 0.85 nouns, 0.89 predicates), a much smaller but highly reliable noun/predicate-separating F2 (noun mean 0.076, predicate mean -0.116; Welch t = 30.6, p < .0001), and the cleanest F1/F2 orthogonality of the three languages so far (r = -0.002, vs. Japanese’s -0.015 and Cantonese’s 0.234).

3. Confirmatory bifactor model

bifactor_items %>%
  mutate(own_specific = if_else(pos2 == "noun", S1_noun, S2_predicate)) %>%
  group_by(pos2) %>%
  summarise(mean_G = mean(G), mean_own_specific = mean(own_specific), n = n()) %>%
  kable(digits = 2, caption = "Mean general (G) and own-specific-factor loadings by item type.") %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
Mean general (G) and own-specific-factor loadings by item type.
pos2 mean_G mean_own_specific n
noun 3.17 1.01 312
predicate 3.86 1.42 166

One caveat worth flagging before trusting these numbers: mirt printed a warning during this fit (“Log-likelihood was decreasing near the ML solution. EM method may be unstable”). Item parameters were checked for anything degenerate (extreme loadings, near-zero/boundary values) and none were found; the CAT simulation below (Section 4) also ultimately recovers the full-bank bias estimate at r = .98 given enough items, which would be hard to explain if the fit had actually landed somewhere badly wrong. Still, a from-different-starting-values refit would be worth doing before treating these English item parameters as final, since this is the only one of the three language fits that raised this warning.

rel <- empirical_rxx(bifactor_scores %>%
                        select(G, S1_noun, S2_predicate, SE_G, SE_S1_noun, SE_S2_predicate) %>%
                        as.matrix())
tibble(dimension = names(rel), empirical_rxx = rel) %>%
  kable(digits = 2, caption = "Empirical reliability of full-item-bank (non-adaptive) factor scores, on the n=1500 subsample.") %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
Empirical reliability of full-item-bank (non-adaptive) factor scores, on the n=1500 subsample.
dimension empirical_rxx
G 0.97
S1_noun 0.80
S2_predicate 0.74 
ggplot(bifactor_scores, aes(x = production, y = noun_predicate_bias)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.1) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE) +
  labs(x = "Total production (sum score)", y = "Noun/predicate bias (S1 - S2)",
       title = sprintf("r = %.2f", cor(bifactor_scores$production, bifactor_scores$noun_predicate_bias))) +
  theme_bw()

The bias score decouples from vocabulary size here too – in fact more cleanly than either other language: r = -0.06 with production (Japanese: -.16, Cantonese: -.11) and r = -0.13 with age. The S1/S2 EAP score correlation is 0.59 – between Japanese’s .48 and Cantonese’s .72.

4. CAT simulation

Drule again matched-or-beat Wrule on a subsample check and was used throughout. min_SEM was set adaptively from this dataset’s own full-bank SE ceiling (0.4 / 0.39 for S1/S2) rather than reused from another language – the Cantonese replication had already shown that reusing another language’s target badly under-shoots.

cat_summary %>%
  kable(digits = 3, caption = "English CAT simulation: item budget vs. recovered precision.") %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
English CAT simulation: item budget vs. recovered precision.
criteria max_items mean_n_items mean_SE_G mean_SE_S1 mean_SE_S2 r_bias_vs_full r_G_vs_full n_items_never_used
Drule 50 48.286 0.207 0.537 0.529 0.819 0.985 215
Drule 100 80.139 0.190 0.506 0.501 0.884 0.990 69
Drule 200 131.964 0.182 0.492 0.488 0.916 0.993 2
Drule (min_items=200 forced) 250 245.430 0.160 0.445 0.459 0.981 NA NA

Even with the adaptively-set target, recovery at a 200-item cap (mean 132 items administered) was weaker than either other language (r = .92, vs. Japanese’s .95 and Cantonese’s .97 at similar or smaller item counts). Forcing more items (min_items = 200, tightened min_SEM = c(0.3,0.3,0.3), capped at 250) resolved this the same way it did for Cantonese: mean items rose to 245, and r(CAT bias, full-bank bias) reached .98 – the best of the three languages once given enough items. So this was again a stopping-rule calibration issue, not evidence that the flagged convergence warning compromised the model.

5. Three-language comparison

tibble(
  language = c("Japanese", "Cantonese", "English (American)"),
  n_for_modeling = c(nrow(jp_bifactor_scores), nrow(can_bifactor_scores), nrow(bifactor_scores)),
  n_available = c(nrow(jp_bifactor_scores), nrow(can_bifactor_scores), nrow(resp_data$d_demo)),
  n_content_items = c(478, 572, 478),
  full_bank_reliability_S1 = c(0.71, 0.86, 0.80),
  full_bank_reliability_S2 = c(0.64, 0.80, 0.74),
  bias_vs_production_r = c(
    round(cor(jp_bifactor_scores$production, jp_bifactor_scores$S1_noun - jp_bifactor_scores$S2_predicate), 2),
    round(cor(can_bifactor_scores$production, can_bifactor_scores$noun_predicate_bias), 2),
    round(cor(bifactor_scores$production, bifactor_scores$noun_predicate_bias), 2)
  ),
  best_cat_recovery_r = c(0.95, 0.97, 0.98),
  items_for_best_recovery = c(131, 192, 245)
) %>%
  kable(digits = 2, caption = "Japanese vs. Cantonese vs. English: key numbers side by side.") %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
Japanese vs. Cantonese vs. English: key numbers side by side.
language n_for_modeling n_available n_content_items full_bank_reliability_S1 full_bank_reliability_S2 bias_vs_production_r best_cat_recovery_r items_for_best_recovery
Japanese 939 939 478 0.71 0.64 -0.16 0.95 131
Cantonese 1205 1205 572 0.86 0.80 -0.11 0.97 192
English (American) 1500 8998 478 0.80 0.74 -0.06 0.98 245

The bifactor design and Drule-based CAT transfer across all three languages tested. One consistent methodological lesson emerged from doing this three times: an empirically-set min_SEM stopping target still isn’t enough on its own – Cantonese and English both showed the CAT stopping well short of the item counts actually needed for high-fidelity bias recovery, even with a target calibrated to that dataset’s own precision ceiling. A substantial min_items floor (on the order of 150-250, well above what’s needed for general ability alone) currently seems necessary in all three languages to reliably reach r > .95 against the full item bank.

6. Open questions

  1. Bifactor refit stability: worth a from-different-starting-values refit of the English model given the convergence warning, even though downstream checks suggest it isn’t consequential.
  2. Full-sample refit: the n=1500 subsample was a tractability call; with ~9000 administrations available, a full-sample (or larger subsample) refit would tighten these estimates further and is easy to justify given how promising the subsampled results are.
  3. Given the min_items floor needed for good recovery (150-250) is much longer than the existing unidimensional production CATs (~25-50 items), is a combined single-session CAT (general ability + bias, sharing items) preferable to a separate, longer bias-specific instrument, across all three languages?
  4. The multidim_pipeline/lib.R refactor means adding a fourth language is now mostly: pull data, check the category mapping needs no additions, decide on a subsample size if N is large, and run. Worth deciding whether further languages are wanted before over-investing in generalizing further (e.g. automatic WG+WS reconciliation, which was skipped here since English’s WS-only sample was already large enough).
